ISOLATED HYPERTROPHY OF THE TIBIALIS
ANTERIOR MUSCLE IN THE STIFF LEG
SYNDROME
A 63-year-old woman with a medic al history of insulin-
dependent diabetes mellitus and pernicious anemia
presented with progressive continous stiffness and superim-
posed painful spasms in the left leg for 3 years. Her symp-
toms were often triggered by su dden auditory and tactile
stimuli or by emotional stress. These symptoms resulted in
walking difﬁculties and limitations in daily activities.
Clinical examination showed abnormal posturing of
the left ankle. It was slightly dorsiﬂexed, and active and
passive ankle movements were severely limited due to
associated pain. There was striking isolated hypertrophy
of the left tibialis anterior muscle. There were no signs
of truncal rigidity or lumbar hyperlordosis.
Brain and spinal MRI were normal. EMG showed a typ-
ical pattern of continuous low-frequency ﬁring of normal
motor unit potentials indistinguishable from voluntary
muscle contraction in the tibialis anterior muscle, without
concomitant antagonist muscle activation, despite attempts
at muscle relaxation by the patient. Sudden auditory and
tactile stimuli could not provoke muscle spasms during
EMG examination. EMG of the abdominal, paraspinal,
and other limb muscles showed no abnormalities. Because
stiff leg syndrome was suspect ed, antiglutamic acid decar-
boxylase (GAD) antibodies were assayed and found to be
highly increased (>2000 U/ml; normal <5 U/ml). Insulin
and islet cell antibodies were not measured.
MRI of the lower limbs conﬁrmed isolated hypertro-
phy of the tibialis anterior muscle (Fig. 1). Cerebrospi-
nal ﬂuid (CSF) analysis was normal, and there were no
oligoclonal bands. Diazepam 5 mg twice daily and
monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions led to
signiﬁcant clinical improvement. A diagnosis of stiff leg
syndrome was made.
To the best of our knowledge, muscle hypertrophy has
never been described in the stiff person or stiff leg syn-
drome. Several cases of stiff person syndrome were
reported with symptoms conﬁned to one (most often dis-
tal) limb, usually the lower leg.
1,2 The spasms are sponta-
neous, reﬂex-induced, or induced by voluntary movement,
in the absence of truncal rigidity or exaggerated lumbar
lordosis. In contrast to the typical stiff person syndrome,
serum/CSF anti-GAD antibodies and oligoclonal bands in
the CSF are most often absent in the stiff limb syndrome,
making a deﬁnitive diagnosis sometimes difﬁcult.
3
Isolated tibialis anterior muscle hypertrophy in our
patient seemed to be related to persistent muscle con-
traction, as has been seen in other muscle disorders
associated with involuntary muscle contraction (e.g.,
myotonic syndromes, rippling muscle syndrome, and
dystonia).
Giovanni Castelnovo, MD
Dimitri Renard, MD
Stephane Bouly, MD
Pierre Labauge, MD, PhD
